title: Calling Conventions & Stack Frames
summary: The agreed contract that lets separately-compiled functions call each other correctly, and how a stack frame is laid out.

slides.markdown:
A **calling convention** is an agreed contract — where arguments go, where the return value goes, who cleans up the stack — that lets code compiled **independently, even by different compilers**, call into each other correctly.

Without it, a library compiled with one compiler couldn't safely be called from code compiled by another: each side needs to make the *exact same* assumptions about where to find arguments and how to hand back a result. This is why calling conventions are part of an ABI (application binary interface) — the binary-level counterpart to an API.

Each function call gets its own **stack frame** — a region of the call stack holding everything that call needs:

![Stack frame layout showing return address, saved registers, local variables, and arguments, growing downward](assets/stack-frame-layout.svg)

Frames stack on top of each other as calls nest, and each one is torn down the moment its function returns — which is exactly why a local variable's address becomes invalid the instant its function exits.

assets.alt: Stack frame layout showing return address, saved registers, local variables, and arguments, growing downward

slides.markdown:
Modern calling conventions pass the **first several arguments in registers** (fast, no memory access) and **spill the rest onto the stack** once registers run out — x86-64's System V ABI, for instance, uses six integer registers before falling back to the stack.

This is a deliberate speed optimization over older conventions that pushed *everything* onto the stack: most functions take few enough arguments that they never touch memory at all for argument passing, which matters because function calls are extremely frequent.

Not every register survives a function call automatically — the convention splits registers into two groups:

- **Caller-saved (volatile)** — the *caller* must save these before the call if it needs their values afterward; the callee is free to overwrite them.
- **Callee-saved (non-volatile)** — the *callee* must restore these to their original values before returning, even if it uses them internally.

This split avoids wasted work: registers used purely as scratch by short-lived calls don't need saving by anyone, while long-lived values across a call are protected without every single register needing a save on every call.

Every function begins with a **prologue** — saving the caller's frame pointer, allocating space for locals, saving any callee-saved registers it will use — and ends with an **epilogue** that reverses exactly that, then returns.

```asm
push  rbp          ; prologue: save caller's frame pointer
mov   rbp, rsp     ; prologue: establish new frame pointer
sub   rsp, 16      ; prologue: reserve space for locals
...
mov   rsp, rbp      ; epilogue: deallocate locals
pop   rbp           ; epilogue: restore caller's frame pointer
ret                 ; return to caller
```

This symmetric setup/teardown is what makes stack frames composable no matter how deeply calls nest.

Each recursive call to `factorial(n)` gets its **own, independent frame** — this is precisely why recursion doesn't corrupt earlier calls' local variables:

```
factorial(3) frame: n=3, return addr = caller
  -> factorial(2) frame: n=2, return addr = factorial(3)'s call site
    -> factorial(1) frame: n=1, return addr = factorial(2)'s call site
      -> base case returns 1
    <- factorial(2) computes 2*1=2, returns, frame destroyed
  <- factorial(3) computes 3*2=6, returns, frame destroyed
```

The stack literally grows one frame per recursive call — which is exactly why unbounded recursion causes a **stack overflow**: each frame consumes real memory until the stack region runs out.

slides.subTitle: Stack-based buffer overflow
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A local array overflowing just corrupts other local variables — annoying, but harmless."

**Why it's wrong:** locals typically sit *below* the saved return address on the stack. An unchecked write past the end of a local buffer (e.g., `strcpy` into a fixed-size array) can overwrite the **saved return address itself** — letting an attacker redirect execution to arbitrary code the moment the function returns.

**Correct model:** this is the classic stack-based buffer overflow, one of the oldest and most consequential memory-safety bugs — the reason stack canaries, ASLR, and non-executable stacks all exist. (Cross-link: Security → application security.)
